content: 1. Studies conducted in Tanzania, Ghana, Malawi, South Africa, and Bissau have reported varying sensitivities for diagnostic tests, ranging from 62% to 100%. This inconsistency may be attributed to differences in specimen type, specimen processing, and study populations. Two studies demonstrated very high sensitivities (100% and 96%), while others reported lower sensitivities (62–70%). 2. Specificities of the tests ranged from 99% to 100%, with minimal heterogeneity observed. Confidence intervals were narrow, indicating precision in specificity estimates. 3. The diagnostic accuracy of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) assays was evaluated using both rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and enzyme immunoassays (EIAs) against reference standards. Sensitivity estimates for both RDTs and EIAs showed significant heterogeneity, while specificity estimates were more consistent. 4. Heterogeneity in sensitivity may arise from the use of different reference standards, variations in clinical subgroups (e.g., children vs. adults), patient status, and disease stage. RDTs were slightly inferior to EIAs in sensitivity when compared to reference standards. 5. In HIV-positive patients, RDTs demonstrated reduced sensitivity, possibly due to the increased prevalence of occult hepatitis B in this population. Occult hepatitis B is characterized by low HBV DNA levels and may evade detection by standard assays. 6. Pre-transfusion screening of blood donations in resource-limited settings remains a significant public health challenge. RDTs used in these settings often exhibit suboptimal sensitivity, with high false-negative rates attributed to operator error, low HBsAg levels, assay degradation, or lot variation. 7. Whole blood samples (capillary and venous) showed marginally better accuracy for RDTs compared to serum samples. However, operational challenges in resource-limited settings, such as transportation and quality assurance, may impact test performance. 8. Analytical sensitivity of different assays contributes to heterogeneity in results. Lower limits of detection (LOD) vary among assays, and insufficient data prevent stratification of results based on LOD. 9. False negatives in HBsAg detection are often associated with low antigen levels and inactive disease. In some cases, patients with false-negative results may still require antiviral therapy due to evidence of fibrosis. 10. False positives have been observed in vaccinated individuals and those with resolved infections. Interestingly, all false negatives were positive for hepatitis B core antibody (HBcAb), suggesting low antigenemia or early infection. 11. Studies evaluating RDTs and EIAs have reported conflicting results, with some assays demonstrating significant differences in sensitivity. Variability in results may be influenced by factors such as the prozone effect, genotype variations, and manufacturing changes. 12. The World Health Organization (WHO) emphasizes the importance of timely global testing, prevention, and treatment of hepatitis B. While RDTs have limitations, they remain a critical tool in resource-limited settings where laboratory capacity is insufficient. 13. The natural history of hepatitis B, including progression and infectiousness, is being investigated for correlations with quantitative HBsAg, HBeAg, and HBV DNA levels. Low levels of these markers may not always indicate clinically significant disease. 14. Statistical heterogeneity remains a challenge in diagnostic accuracy reviews. Despite stratified analyses, no single factor fully explains the observed variability in sensitivity and specificity. 15. Limitations of the meta-analysis include the exclusion of non-English studies, potential publication bias, and reliance on case-control designs or preselected cohorts, which may introduce bias. Additionally, insufficient data on serological markers and genotypes limit the ability to correlate heterogeneity with disease stages and severity. 16. The evolving nature of HBV mutants and the lack of standardized reference assays further complicate diagnostic accuracy studies. Occult hepatitis B and low antigen levels present additional challenges for accurate diagnosis. 17. The WHO underscores the need for improved diagnostic tools and strategies to address the global burden of hepatitis B, particularly in high-prevalence regions and resource-limited settings.
